step_by_step_reasoning: The architecture depicts Infinitium's Fraud Detection System (FDS 2.0) on AWS. Entry starts at an external Authentication System which sends payment authentication requests through Amazon CloudFront. AWS WAF evaluates CloudFront traffic against web vulnerabilities. Requests are then routed from CloudFront to Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), which distributes traffic into an ECS Cluster powered by AWS Fargate running Graviton instances. Container images are deployed into Amazon ECR via CI/CD and pulled by AWS Fargate. Fargate microservices query distinct database substrates based on workload requirements: Amazon Neptune for graph-based historical transaction analysis and velocity metrics, Amazon RDS for organizational/user CMS data, Amazon DocumentDB for storing 290+ fraud policies and rules, and Amazon MemoryDB for Redis for microsecond-latency caching of authentication tokens.

nodes.name: Authentication System
nodes.notes: External payment authentication system initiating payment transaction requests.

nodes.name: Amazon CloudFront
nodes.notes: Global CDN entry point delivering low-latency request routing across the region.

nodes.name: AWS WAF
nodes.notes: Web Application Firewall protecting CloudFront against common vulnerabilities.

nodes.name: Elastic Load Balancing
nodes.notes: Load balancer handling incoming scalability and routing traffic to container tasks.

nodes.name: AWS Fargate
nodes.notes: Serverless container compute inside the ECS cluster running microservices on Graviton instances.

nodes.name: Amazon ECR
nodes.notes: Container registry storing microservice images built through the CI/CD pipeline.

nodes.name: Amazon Neptune
nodes.notes: Graph database managing interconnected transaction, user, and device data as well as historic velocity metrics.

nodes.name: Amazon RDS
nodes.notes: Relational database storing traditional organizational and user CMS data.

nodes.name: Amazon DocumentDB
nodes.notes: Document database storing rules and over 290 fraud detection policies.

nodes.name: Amazon MemoryDB for Redis
nodes.notes: In-memory database providing microsecond latency for microservice authentication token lookup.

edges.notes: Authentication System sends payment transaction request to CloudFront.
CloudFront passes request through AWS WAF for security inspection.
CloudFront routes validated traffic to Elastic Load Balancing.
Elastic Load Balancing distributes requests to AWS Fargate instances in the ECS Cluster.
AWS Fargate pulls container microservice images from Amazon ECR.
Fargate queries Neptune graph database for transaction velocity and historical relationship insights.
Fargate accesses Amazon RDS for organizational and user CMS interface information.
Fargate reads and flattens fraud rules/policies stored in Amazon DocumentDB.
Fargate checks and caches authentication session state in Amazon MemoryDB for Redis at microsecond speed.
